meta.title: Who really said "The arts are not a way to make a living. They are a very human way of making life more bearable"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Vonnegut — A Man Without a Country (2005), p. 24. The line usually arrives without the joke and the instruction that surround it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The arts are not a way to make a living. They are a very human way of making life more bearable'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Vonnegut, from A Man Without a Country (2005). Quoted alone it sounds resigned; in the essay it is an order to go and make something.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Vonnegut, and precisely locatable: the essay “Here is a lesson in creative writing” in A Man Without a Country (New York: Seven Stories Press, 2005), page 24. Two sentences that are almost always lifted out of a passage telling the reader to sing in the shower and write a lousy poem for a friend.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: A Man Without a Country, essay: “Here is a lesson in creative writing”
2005 — Seven Stories Press, New York; edited by Daniel Simon
p. 24 (verified against scans by Quote Investigator)
The Best American Nonrequired Reading 2006, ed. Dave Eggers, p. 348

source.excerpt: The arts are not a way to make a living. They are a very human way of making life more bearable. Practicing an art, no matter how well or badly, is a way to make your soul grow, for heaven’s sake. Sing in the shower. Dance to the radio. Tell stories. Write a poem to a friend, even a lousy poem. Do it as well as you possibly can. You will get an enormous reward. You will have created something.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ located the quotation and verified it against scans: A Man Without a Country, edited by Daniel Simon, chapter “Here is a lesson in creative writing,” p. 24 (Seven Stories Press, New York, 2005).
Wikiquote’s sourced Vonnegut page ↗ independently lists the full passage under A Man Without a Country (2005), including the sentences that follow.
Quote Investigator ↗ traces the reprints too — the essay ran again in The Best American Nonrequired Reading (2006), ed. Dave Eggers, p. 348, which is how the passage reached a wider audience.
A physical copy of the 2005 Seven Stories edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗ for anyone who wants to check page 24 against the book.
source.excerptNote: The two famous sentences are the set-up, not the conclusion. Everything after them is an instruction — and the passage opens, in Vonnegut’s usual manner, with a joke about annoying your parents.

author.name: Kurt Vonnegut
author.heading: About Kurt Vonnegut
author.bio: Kurt Vonnegut (1922–2007) was an American novelist and essayist who survived the Allied firebombing of Dresden as a prisoner of war and spent the rest of his career writing about it, obliquely and then directly. Cat’s Cradle, Slaughterhouse-Five and Breakfast of Champions fused science fiction, black comedy and moral seriousness into a voice nobody has successfully imitated. In his last decades he wrote more essays than novels, and became one of the most quoted — and most misquoted — American writers on the internet.

misattribution.heading: Real quote — read the rest of the paragraph
misattribution.intro: The attribution holds up exactly. What the internet does to this one is cut it in half and invert its mood.

items.why: Quoted alone, the two sentences read as consolation for not making money. In the essay they are followed immediately by orders: practise an art anyway, “no matter how well or badly”; sing in the shower; write a lousy poem for a friend. Quote Investigator ↗ prints the whole passage.
The passage opens with a gag about wanting to hurt your parents, which sets the register. Wikiquote ↗ preserves it; motivational graphics almost never do.

items.who: the printed essay, not a speech
items.why: The documented source is the essay “Here is a lesson in creative writing” in A Man Without a Country (2005), p. 24 ↗, which Quote Investigator ↗ verified against scans. Vonnegut gave a great many commencement addresses and reused his material freely, so a line like this is easy to take for speech material — but the page you can check is the printed one.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: really Vonnegut — A Man Without a Country ↗, p. 24, 2005 — and the sentence after it is the one doing the work.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Vonnegut was eighty-two and writing what turned out to be his last book, a short, cranky, funny collection of essays about America, war, oil and his own decline. This passage is the closest the book comes to advice.

The argument is a deliberate demotion. Art is not a career and not a talent contest — it is a household activity, like exercise, that makes a person more bearable to themselves. Which is why he immediately reduces the stakes to singing in the shower.
detailsBody: The essay was reprinted the following year in The Best American Nonrequired Reading, edited by Dave Eggers, and the two sentences have since been anthologised into writing guides, Forbes’s quotations page and at least one advice compendium — usually stripped of the instructions that make them a programme rather than a sentiment.
context.pull: “Practicing an art, no matter how well or badly, is a way to make your soul grow, for heaven’s sake.”
